To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the BRCA1 and 2 genes are the most common cause of familial breast and ovarian cancer, but that the genes account for less than 10% of all breast cancer cases and less than 20% of all ovarian cancer cases, and that the lifetime risk of developing cancer for carriers is 50% to 80% for breast cancer, 10% to 40% for ovarian cancer and 5% to 20% for other cancers.

1) the majority of women with hereditary breast and/or ovarian cancer have mutations in BRCA genes; 2) the risk of breast and/or ovarian carcinoma associated with mutations in these genes is high; and 3) women with hereditary cancer have options to reduce their risk of cancer, which include surveillance, chemoprerevention and prophylaxis.
the BRCA1 and the BRCA2 gene mutations are associated with increased risk of breast and ovary cancers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of genes that are responsible for the development of breast cancer.
the role of oncologist in identifying and managing the patients with hereditary breast and ovary cancer risk.
the development of new methods for the treatment of cancer, and the development of new drugs for the treatment of breast and prostate cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the American Society of Clinical oncology has affirmed the important role of clinical oncologist in identifying and managing the patients with familial cancer.

the American Society of Clinical oncologists has affirmed the role and importance of clinical oncologists and other medical specialists in the identification and management of patients with familial cancer risks.
the oncologist should be the first person to identify the hereditary risk of the patient, and then the oncologist should refer the patient to a geneticist or other genetic specialist.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of breast or ovarian cancer is increased for a woman whose family has one or more cases of breast cancer, ovarian cancer, or both.
the oncology community is well positioned to address the needs of patients with hereditary cancer risk.
we have identified a novel gene, BRCA1, which is involved in the pathogenesis of a large fraction of familial breast cancer and which is mutated in a significant fraction of sporadic breast cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there is a need to improve our understanding of the role of genetic testing for hereditary breast cancer in clinical practice, including how to best communicate genetic test results, and how to best use genetic test results to inform clinical management.

the majority of women with a family history of breast and/or ovarian cancer do not have a BRCA mutation and that the risk of cancer for women with a family cancer history is much less than the general population.
we have identified a new mechanism that is important for the development of breast cancer.
